entities.name: Adélard Langevin
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Adélard Langevin (1855–1915) was a Canadian Oblate of Mary Immaculate who served as the first Archbishop of Saint-Boniface in Manitoba, becoming the most prominent Catholic defender of French-Canadian language rights in the Canadian West during one of the country's most acrimonious educational controversies. Born in Quebec, he joined the Oblates and was appointed to Saint-Boniface in 1895.

Langevin's archiepiscopal career was dominated by the Manitoba Schools Question—a prolonged legal and political battle over the rights of Catholic and French-speaking minority populations to maintain publicly funded denominational schools. The 1890 Manitoba Schools Act stripped Catholic and French schools of their public funding, provoking a bitter national controversy. Langevin became the most vocal and tenacious Catholic advocate for the restoration of minority school rights, engaging in campaigns, petitions, and political lobbying at both provincial and federal levels.

Despite failing to achieve full restoration of Catholic school rights, his campaign established the principle of minority language and religious school rights as a constitutional issue in Canadian public life. He is remembered as a champion of French-Canadian rights in the West and as an embodiment of the Oblate missionary commitment to the Métis and French-Canadian communities of the Canadian prairies. Saint-Boniface and the larger Francophone Catholic community of Manitoba trace their institutional resilience in part to his determined advocacy.

entities.name: Adélard Langevin
entities.label: Person
entities.summary: Louis Philippe Adélard Langevin was a Canadian Oblate priest and Archbishop of Saint-Boniface. He founded the La Liberté newspaper published in Manitoba on May 20, 1913. He was the energetic leader of the Catholic struggle to restore language and religious rights in the Manitoba Schools Question.
